en: The Extensive Explanation and Resolution of the *Mahāyānacaturdharmasūtra-śāstra*:
On What Does One Rely for Abiding? When the World-Honored One was in the world, he himself disciplined those who were wicked;
after his parinirvāṇa, how should one dwell together? While the Tathāgata was present, the Buddha himself expounded the sūtras; after his parinirvāṇa, all...
What words should be placed at the beginning of this sutra so that sentient beings may have faith?
The World-Honored One said:
"After my parinirvāṇa,
take the precepts as your teacher."
To sever all evil and give rise to all goodness—
were I to remain in the world, it would be no different.
Therefore, one should dwell with focused attention upon the four foundations of mindfulness,
contemplating the impurity of the body.
Contemplate that feelings are suffering;
contemplate that the mind is impermanent;
contemplate that phenomena are non-self.
Thus, one eliminates the four inversions;
having emerged from birth and death,
one attains the realization of the noble path.
Therefore, one should always abide by this.
When wicked bhikṣus are dealt with through the Brahma-penance (brahmadanda), one should simply not speak with them; they shall be subdued by this declaration.
The words "Thus have I heard" and so forth should be placed at the beginning of all sutras;
thus will sentient beings have faith.
This was due to the request of Kāśyapa.
The inclusion of this passage constitutes the reason for its origin within this context. To clarify the underlying purpose,
there are briefly four meanings.
First, to eliminate doubt;
second, to inspire faith;
and third, to distinguish the heterodox.
Fourth is to manifest the correct [teaching] and eliminate doubts;
this is stated in the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*: [Text follows...]
At the time of the council,
Ānanda ascended the seat;
through the majestic power of the Dharma, his appearance suddenly became like that of the Buddha.
The assembly gave rise to three doubts:
first, the doubt that Great Compassion had arisen from nirvana;
second, the doubt that a distinct Buddha had come from another direction.
Third, he severed the doubt that Ānanda would turn his body and become a Buddha;
having thus severed these three doubts together,
it is said that "faith was born."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"This is taught in order to inspire faith in the time, the place, and the people."
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith;
furthermore, it is because faith is the source of the Way and the mother of its attainment.
To rescue and deliver sentient beings from birth and death,
one must first raise the hand of faith and bestow the hand of the teaching.
The hand that gives rise to faith and the hand of the orthodox teaching join their palms together.
Because one has emerged from the mire;
it is like a person who, having hands,
goes to a mountain to retrieve treasures.
If one has no hands, one will obtain nothing from emptiness;
yet so it is for those who possess faith.
By entering the Dharma, one attains realization;
yet for those without faith,
even understanding is of no benefit.
Therefore, at the beginning of the sutra, one is led to generate pure faith;
as for the statement "excluding the heterodox," it simply means that such sixfold textual passages do not exist [in those systems].
One should know that these are all subsumed within the teachings of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
For instance, at the beginning of all non-Buddhist scriptures, the two characters "A" and "U" are invariably placed;
here, "A" symbolizes non-existence (abhāva).
The term "bubble" (au) signifies existence;
it indicates that the purport of this teaching does not depart from existence and non-existence.
Now, the six propositions are set aside in order to distinguish [this teaching] from them.

Because the Three Jewels are most auspicious,

as for the explanation of the main text,

First, faith;

Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of initial faith," the Sūtra says: "Thus [it is].
This cites the Dharma that has been heard.
Causing sentient beings to have faith is called "accomplishment of faith.
Now, setting aside various other explanations, I shall interpret it through three meanings.
First, each of the two characters is explained individually;
next, the meaning of the two characters is presented collectively;
finally, "evam" is interpreted by incorporating "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam).
Regarding the initial statement on "individual explanations," there have been many interpretations since antiquity;
their general purport does not deviate from the categories of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
Therefore, I shall now explain it based on these four meanings.
The teaching is able to manifest the principle;
as for the phrase "seeking the meaning according to the text," this refers to that very point.
Principle accords with reality and teaching reveals it—this is "as-it-is" (tathatā).
Meaning does not deviate from the text and the text is called "correct"—this is "as-it-is.
Relying on the teaching to initiate practice is "as-it-is."
Conformity with principle through the three characteristics is "is-ness" (yathābhūta).
Attaining the fruit based on the cause is "suchness" (tathatā).
Correspondence of the cause to the fruit is "is-ness" (yathā).
Next, regarding the term "general declaration" (saṃnipāta):
it is stated as "Thus" (evam) because this sutra is shown to be free from four kinds of faults.
First, it is free from the fault of being a self-proclamation, for the Dharma spoken by the Buddha is exactly thus.
Second, regarding the removal of aging, the phrasing and meaning are definitively established as being thus for all.
Therefore, those who do not believe [this] are so; yet if there are those who do believe, [they shall attain it].
Because it is said to be "thus.

the subsequent remark, "I have heard that the explanation is thus," is made in accordance with the intent of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and various commentaries.
Thus, this general statement functions according to four meanings.
First, it relies on question and answer to demonstrate the avoidance of the faults of self-proclamation and hearsay;
that is to say, at the time of the compilation, the assembly posed a question, saying:
Because it was heard previously exactly as it was spoken, he replied, "Thus have I heard.
Second, by means of a simile, he demonstrates the avoidance of the faults of exaggeration and deficiency. That is to say:
The fact that the words spoken are exactly as he heard them in the past, and that they shall be spoken up to this point without any deviation,
demonstrates his quality of mastery and capability through the granting of permission.
The assembly all requested him to speak,

you should speak thus."

"I shall speak thus, exactly as I have heard it.
By teaching according to these four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), he demonstrates the merit of inspiring reverence, faith, and acceptance.
Thus did the assembly of monks at the auspicious council declare:
"Listen now to what I have heard; you should listen correctly and practice according to the truth."
Regarding the second point, the accomplishment of "hearing":
the Sūtra says, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), which names the person who hears.
To manifest that one has heard it directly from the source is the accomplishment of hearing;
this refers to the transmitter of the Dharma.
Referring to one's own body, he says: "Such is the Dharma;
I have heard it directly from myself.
Here, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the conventional person (*pudgala*) as a composite of the aggregates (*skandha*), which is designated as "self" because it possesses a governing cause.
"Listening" refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness to hear sounds;
the mental faculty follows the auditory consciousness to apprehend the names and so forth produced by those sounds,
which then perfume the consciousness as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The collective manifestation is generally termed "hearing" (*śruta*); setting aside the particulars,
one adopts the general designation.
Therefore, it is called "I have heard the question.
Why is it necessary to set aside the specific and answer in general terms?
It is to demonstrate that [understanding] relies upon various conditions.
This means that when hearing the Dharma, one must possess mental attention (*cittālambana*).
If every single detail were set forth, it would become overly prolix;
therefore, only one point is raised here.

It is by relying on the various conditions that one says, "I have heard.
If this is so, why not say, "There is no 'I' who has heard"?
Answer: It is to eliminate fear,
lest the various non-Buddhists and others hear the sound of "non-self" [and be terrified].
Since it has been stated that there is no self,
who is it that hears and who is it that studies,
and who is it that fears the Buddha-dharma?
Because there is no entering from behind.
There is further question and answer,
as clarified in other places.
Regarding the accomplishment of the time of the three [aspects],

It is perfectly suited to the occasion and free from any untimely error;
this is the perfection of timing, meaning that it is clearly taught at the appropriate moment for this specific sūtra.
At one time it was heard that this was spoken in a certain household;

Although it is said to be simultaneous,

As for the term "Bhagavat":
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The term *bhagavat* functions according to six meanings.
First, the meaning of mastery (*vaśitva*)."
Second, the sense of blazing intensity;
third, the sense of sublime majesty;

The meaning of the five auspiciousnesses;
the meaning of nobility. As a verse says:
Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical excellence;

the bodies of all Tathāgatas are not bound by any afflictions.

The māra of afflictions,

Regarding the Māra of the Lord of Sovereignty: the Buddha possesses ten kinds of meritorious names and titles.
For what reason do those who transmit the Dharma according to the Tathāgata’s teachings place only the name "Bhagavān" at the beginning of all sūtras?
That is to say:
because this single name is universally honored by the world,
all non-Buddhists likewise address their own teachers as Bhagavat.
Furthermore, this single name subsumes all virtues, whereas other names do not;
therefore, this name is placed at the beginning of every sutra.
Now, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses three bodies.
This present sutra was spoken by the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya).
If it were addressed to those prior to the stages (bhūmi), it would have been spoken by the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya).
As for those on the ground,
it is taught according to their bodies; as for the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, it is taught according to their dharmas.
Furthermore, there is no preaching of the Dharma;

since the three bodies are non-different in essence.

The term "supreme sprout" refers to the name of the second stage, the Stainless (Vimalā),
because it arises by taking the sprouts of the first and second stages as its cause.
The phrase "supreme among speech" refers to the name of the third bhūmi, the Radiant (Prabhākari),
which is the very sprout of that [wisdom].
In this stage, there is no impairment;
one gradually causes [the qualities] to increase and progress.
Because it leads toward the great fruit,
"endowed with valor" refers to the name of the fourth stage,
the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*jvalanā-prajñā-bhūmi*).
Because within this stage one is able to fully possess the great power of striving for enlightenment,
it is called "and marvelous."
This refers to the name of the fifth stage, "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya),
because it is the most supreme stage for transcending the two vehicles.
As for the term "Great Teacher of the Path" (Mahāmārgācārya):
This refers to the name of the sixth stage, the "Manifest" (Abhimukhī).
It is so named because, by means of realizing the meaning of the profound Prajñāpāramitā,
one is able to guide and benefit all deluded beings.
The term "Great Renown" refers to the name of the seventh stage, Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching).
It is so called because one is able to reach the ultimate perfection of application and thereby possesses great renown.
Regarding the "perfection of great compassion," this refers to the name of the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā).
It is so called because one arises from meditative equipoise in tranquility for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The term "Great Field of Merit" refers to the name of the ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*),
because it is able to fully possess the four kinds of unhindered eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
He preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
because he attains great merit,
it is said that one who is thus fully endowed with the Dharma possesses such mastery.
These two constitute the name of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā).
This is because one is born into the abode of Maheśvara and is able to realize the great dharma-knowledge.

One is able to practice the conduct of enlightenment oneself,
and is also able to perform beneficial deeds for others.
As for what is called the "object-condition of enlightenment":

As for what are called the "merits of awakening," it means:
It is excellent in the beginning, middle,

This surpasses the two vehicles as well as humans and devas.

Because they are able to raise charges against faults;

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"What is endurance? It is as follows:"
It is as if there is one who, when reviled, does not revile in return;
when met with anger, does not respond with anger;
and when struck, does not strike back.
He does not retaliate when struck or provoked.
Furthermore, that venerable one is capable of enduring cold and heat, hunger and thirst.
Mosquitoes, gadflies, and lice said:
"We can endure the venomous touch of snakes and hedgehogs,
as well as the harsh and abusive words and syllables uttered by others against us."
Furthermore, one is able to reflect upon and endure all the intense, rigid, and piercing sufferings within the body— agonizing sensations that cut to the heart and snatch away life—
which one must bear and accept.
This is called "endurance.
The explanation states:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks:

Suppose there is someone who, toward the Great Teacher and others,
is fully endowed with compassionate physical action,
fully endowed with compassionate verbal action, and fully endowed with compassionate mental action.
One should share and enjoy with fellow practitioners of wisdom whatever is to be enjoyed;
all food and drink should be taken without secrecy,

Whatever is obtained in accordance with the Dharma,
wherever it may be in the bowl,
is contained within the bowl.
And having received the same precepts and the same views,
they achieve these six kinds of qualities that are delightful, acceptable, venerable, and free from conflict—
the nature of being easy to dwell with.
One should not cause distress to others,
nor to those who possess wisdom and are fellow practitioners of the holy life.
To dwell together in one place and always cause others to rejoice—
this is called gentleness (*sauratya*). Thus it is explained.

Therefore, it says at the beginning of the *Pramuditā-bhūmi*:
One fulfills all great vows by means of ten phrases of totality.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
First, the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings;
second, the exhaustion of the world-realm;
third, the exhaustion of the realm of empty space.
Fourth, the exhaustion of the dharma-realm;
fifth, the exhaustion of the nirvana-realm;
sixth, the exhaustion of the worlds in which Buddhas appear.
Seventh, the exhaustion of the realm of the wisdom of the seven Tathāgatas.
Eighth, the exhaustion of the realm of the objects of the mind.
Ninth, the exhaustion of the realm of entry into the wisdom of the Buddha’s sphere.
When the ten worldly realms, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are exhausted;
when the realm of the Tathāgata’s birth is exhausted,
my vows shall likewise be exhausted.
As far as the end of the world-system extends;
as far as the limit of the realm of spiritual space extends;
as far as the limit of the dharma-realm extends.
As the realm of nirvāṇa is inexhaustible;
as the worlds in which Buddhas appear are inexhaustible;
as the realm of a Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible.
As far as the realm of the objects of the mind extends;
as far as the realm of the entry of the Buddha’s wisdom into his sphere extends;
as far as the realms of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom extend.
If that realm were to be exhausted,
I vow to reach its total exhaustion;
such is the question of whether the realm of sentient beings will ever be exhausted or not.
These roots of goodness of mine are likewise inexhaustible.
They are as inexhaustible as the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of the world-realms, the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of the realm of empty space,
and the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of the dharma-realm.
Whether the realm of nirvana is exhausted or inexhaustible;
whether the world in which Buddhas appear is exhausted or inexhaustible;
whether the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is exhausted or inexhaustible.
Whether the realm of mental objects is exhausted or not;
whether the realm of entry into the wisdom of the Buddha’s sphere is exhausted or not;
and whether the realms of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are exhausted or not.

The section on Clarifying the True Doctrine concludes. The third major section, the Section on the Propagation of the Teaching, is further divided into three parts.
First, the conclusion of the Buddha’s transformational work is indicated.
As the sutra says: "At that time, the Bhagavat, having spoken this sutra...
Next, it clarifies that the assembly heard the Dharma together, as the sutra says: "...the assembly of bhikṣus and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Thereafter, they reverently accepted the guidance and followed it,
just as the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, believed, accepted, and practiced accordingly.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Thus have I heard" is intended to engender faith; with faith,
one receives and practices it.
This is for the sake of generating wisdom.
Because there are three purities and excellences as taught by the Buddha,
it causes those who hear it to joyfully practice accordingly.
First, the purity of the speaker,
because they have attained mastery over all phenomena;
second, the purity of that which is spoken.

Third is the purity of attaining the fruit, because one has already abandoned all hindrances and become a vessel for the Dharma, due to the clarity of the essence of reality through the wisdom that knows things as they truly are.
The Buddha taught them correctly, and they received it with hearts free from the stain of disbelief;
they respectfully and compliantly practiced and studied it.
For this reason, it is said: "They believed, accepted, and practiced accordingly."
